The existing wastewater treatment plant was initially constructed in 1961 to provide primary treatment and was later upgraded to provide secondary treatment and disinfection. The plant is now designed to provide secondary treatment for an average of 2.0 million gallons per day (MGD). As indicated in the study “Improving Process Reliability and Performance Through Flow Equalization” (Nolte & Associates, April 1991), the plant can provide secondary treatment for up to 4.4 MGD during wet weather. From April 2015 through November 2019, daily influent flows ranged between 0.10 and 1.6 MGD, with an average of 0.34 MGD. Existing plant operations and processes include preliminary treatment with bar screening and grit removal, primary treatment with primary sedimentation tanks, secondary treatment with trickling filters and secondary sedimentation, disinfection with sodium hypochlorite, and dechlorination with sodium bisulfite. Treated wastewater is routed to Discharge Point No. 001. b. Planned Facility. The Planned Facility will be designed to treat all wastewater to tertiary treatment standards. It is being designed for an average dry weather flow of 1.3 MGD and a peak wet weather flow of 3.9 MGD. Planned Facility operations and processes are anticipated to include an equalization basin for storage of instantaneous peak flows; preliminary treatment, including screening and grit removal; secondary treatment by means of a membrane bioreac

chunks.text: Primary sedimentation is to remove the suspended solids (SS) by controlling the water flow velocity. It is required the settling time of SS shorter than the water travelling time in the tank. The SS with low density (1.1 g/mL and 1.5 g/mL) or small size but high density (1.5 g/mL) is the target pollutants to be removed in primary clarification. Most abundant MPs in the wastewater is PET followed by PE and PP (Fig. 2b ). The density of PET is between 0.96 and 1.45 g/mL. It is predicted that the primary sedimentation would catch the MPs consist of PET. However, PE and PP are difficult to be removed as they have density lower than water. Hence, wastewater containing large amount of moderate-density MPs would have high MPs removal during primary treatment.

The biological processes occurring in both biological reactors are simulated using the IWA Activated Sludge Model No. 1 (ASM1) proposed by [47] . These state variables are linked to eight degradation bioprocesses occurring in biological reactors.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . Table 5 lists several such advanced technologies currently being considered for pilot, demonstration, and full-scale operations in the North America.

chunks.text: A pilot plant comprised of primary (DAF) and secondary treatment unit (two stage trickling filters) was set up by Li et al. (1984) . Each trickling filter was 2.4 m high and consisted of media (surface area-98 m 2 /m 3 ). Around 40-50% oil and grease removal were achieved from DAF system. In case of trickling filters organic matter removal efficiencies were 70-85%. Apart from that, nitrification also resulted, but the process was entirely dependent upon loading rates. Intensive studies by Banks and Wang (2004) have shown that loading rates plays a vital role in biological treatment. Intensive studies conducted by them have shown that the organic matter removal efficiencies were 60-85% when operated at OLRs of 1.2-8.1 kg BOD/ m 3 -d for nine trickling filters.

chunks.text: Membrane bioreactor (MBR) is the combination of a membrane-based filtration process like microfiltration or ultrafiltration systems with a suspended growth biological reactor. Essentially, the membrane system replaces the solids separation function of the secondary clarifiers in conventional activated sludge systems. The MBR technology combines the unit operations of aeration, secondary clarification, and filtration into a single process, producing a high quality effluent, suitable for any discharge and most reuse or recycle applications, while greatly reducing space requirements and under stringent norms. The use of MBRs is a very interesting option for wastewater treatment and reclamation as they combine efficiently the oxidation of organic matter, with suspended solids and nutrient removal (Monclús et al., 2010) and microbial decontamination. Specially it can be the preferred choice, compared to other combination of both conventional or intensive and natural or extensive technologies, when, in addition to water reuse application and microbial quality, other factors such as the land availability, the respective investment or the process reliability are taken into account (Brissaud, 2010; Wintgens et al., 2005) .

chunks.text: For the treatment phase, the actual operational energy use was based on existing secondary treatment at the WWTP, 22 which was augmented with hypothetical typical tertiary treatment processes to achieve adequate water quality for NPR. Additional treatment processes included coagulation and flocculation with appropriate alum doses 35 using rapid sand filtration and chlorination, which were each modeled independently (Figure 2 ). It was assumed that tertiary treatment was constructed at the equivalent scale of the existing plant (241 000 m 3 /day) and that it was not necessary to size for peak flows, as they would receive only secondary treatment water and not be recycled. For the decentralized facilities, it is also appropriate to design based on average flows because the equalization tank at the beginning of the treatment train is sized sufficiently to buffer the daily variations in flow rate. It is not necessary to accommodate increases in flow due to storm events because infiltration and inflow do not occur in building systems. The biosolids resulting from anaerobic digestion at the centralized WWTP were assumed to be disposed in equal parts (by mass) via land application and daily cover at a landfill, with transportation requirements and landfill emissions estimated.

chunks.text: The main objective of primary treatment of wastewater is the removal of settleable organic and inorganic solids by sedimentation and skimming. Here, about 50 to 60% of the total suspended solids (SS), and 65% of the oil and grease are removed along with some organic nitrogen, phosphorous, and heavy metals attached to the solids. However, the colloidal particles and dissolved constituents are not removed in this stage. Generally, gravity separation is employed in this step to separate the biosolids using either coagulation, flocculation, flotation or filtration techniques as seen in Fig. 2 . However, recent innovations in efficient wastewater treatment have brought advancements in this area (Table 4 ). For example, Salsnes filter system reported to have only 1/10th of land requirement and offers 30-60% lower investment and operating costs as compared to a conventional primary treatment system (Trojan Technologies, 2012).

chunks.text: In the activated sludge process the majority of biological solids removed in the secondary sedimentation tank are recycled (returned sludge). The feedback of most of the cell yields from the sedimentation tank encourages rapid adsorption of the pollutants in the incoming settled sewage and also serves to stabilize the operation over a wide range of dilution rates and substrate concentrations imposed by fluctuations in the flow and strength of the wastewater. Secondary treatment processes can remove up to 95 per cent of the BOD and suspended solids entering the process, as well as significant amounts of heavy metals and certain organic compounds which could otherwise cause the deterioration of chemical and ecological quality of receiving waters [10, 53] . Conventional wastewater treatment usually ends with secondary treatment which cannot efficiently remove all the different compounds found in sewage and therefore treated effluents are one of the main sources of persistent micropollutants in the environment [1, 62] . For water reuse, tertiary treatment is needed to provide additional removal of contaminants such as microbial pathogens, particulates, or nutrients, and advanced treatment processes are employed when wastewater is to be reclaimed for reuse, depending on the type of use and quality requirements [49] .

chunks.text: Based on a survey on pre-treatment measures for 17 full-scale AeMBRs, the following information deserves special attention (Itokawa et al., 2008) : 1) grit chamber, coarse and fine screenings are mostly essential for MBR operation to removal grits, large suspended particles and long fibers, with fine screening (3 mm for FS membrane and 0.5-1 mm for HF membrane) installed universally; and 2) using the "by pass sieving" method, which recycles part of the suspended sludge through a sieve, achieves the further removal of unfavorable substances accumulated in the bioreactor. These means can be extended to AnMBRs minimizing the presence of undesirable substances into the bioreactor while with adequate consideration of keeping strict anaerobic environment. A recent novel concept, referred to as wastewater pre-concentration (Ansari et al., 2016) , is still under investigation, but has shown great potential to enhance bioresource recovery and energy generation efficiency (Guven et al., 2019) , accompanied by a low volumetric flow rate and process footprint (Alvarado et al., 2020) .
